title: Can children’s films beat YouTube?
gist: Toy Story 5 has grossed over $1bn globally with a plot in which a tablet called Lily displaces the toys — a screen-scepticism message Disney will monetise on Disney+, which the author flags as an unresolved contradiction. He argues live-action children's cinema is structurally losing to YouTube's instant gratification, with The Magic Faraway Tree the year's exception because its emotional payload lands on the accompanying adults rather than the children.

insights.claim: Toy Story 5 has grossed over a billion dollars globally, matching both its predecessors, with its plot built around a tablet called Lilypad that displaces the toys in eight-year-old Bonnie's affections.
insights.speaker: Alexander Larman
insights.so_what: A third consecutive billion-dollar entry confirms the franchise's durability as a Disney box-office annuity.
insights.quote: To date, the latest Toy Story film has grossed over a billion dollars at the global box office.

insights.claim: Disney is marketing a film that warns screens and social media are dangerous while knowing it will shortly become a key attraction on its own Disney+ subscription app, an unresolved commercial contradiction.
insights.speaker: Alexander Larman
insights.so_what: Anti-screen messaging is a marketing asset for the same firms selling screen time — expect more of this positioning as streaming competes with short-form video.
insights.quote: observing that screens and social media are dangerous while also being aware that this will soon be one of the key attractions on the Disney+ subscription app

insights.claim: Toy Story 5 is engineered to avoid antagonising anyone: the tablet is presented not as a villain but as a misused tool that by the redemptive close facilitates in-person connection between children.
insights.speaker: Alexander Larman
insights.so_what: Maximum-consensus construction is the template for billion-dollar family franchises — no genuine critique survives the four-quadrant test.
insights.quote: Toy Story 5, like all its predecessors, is a precision-engineered exercise in keeping as many people as happy as possible.

themes.theme: YouTube as the real competitor for children's attention

insights.claim: The structural problem for pre-teen cinema is the dual-audience constraint — adults must buy the tickets and attend — which historically produced films that are torture for anyone over puberty and now makes it harder to cut through against YouTube.
insights.speaker: Alexander Larman
insights.so_what: Family film economics depend on satisfying two audiences at once; short-form video only has to satisfy one, a permanent structural advantage.
insights.quote: The difficulty that films aimed at pre-teen audiences have traditionally had is that they need adults to buy the tickets and accompany children to the cinema.
insights.locator: The difficulty that films aimed at pre-teen audiences

insights.claim: Children now dismiss well-reviewed live-action adventure films such as the 2016 Swallows and Amazons as old hat compared with what MrBeast is offering on YouTube, meaning critical acclaim no longer converts into young audiences.
insights.speaker: Alexander Larman
insights.so_what: Critical reception has decoupled from child audience demand — studio greenlight logic for live-action family films is broken.
insights.quote: who believe, rightly or wrongly, that such thrills are old hat when compared to whatever MrBeast is selling on YouTube

insights.claim: Screens and social media will not lose their hold on the young because they cater to instant gratification mindlessly and easily, a mechanism no film can match.
insights.speaker: Alexander Larman
insights.so_what: Bearish on any thesis that a cultural backlash restores children's attention to long-form media; the gratification mechanic wins.
insights.quote: They cater to instant gratification, mindlessly and easily.

themes.theme: What still works: brands, nostalgia and the adult payload

insights.claim: Even a much-loved brand can decay: the third Paddington film drew a more tepid critical and commercial response after moving the bear to Peru and losing the London culture-clash comedy that powered the first two.
insights.speaker: Alexander Larman
insights.so_what: Family-franchise value is tied to a specific comedic premise, not the character IP alone — relocating the setting destroys the mechanism.
insights.quote: the more tepid critical and commercial response directed towards the third Paddington film—in which the bear heads to Peru, thus losing the culture-clash comedy of his life in London—suggests that even a much-loved brand such as this can struggle
insights.locator: There have been some shining examples

insights.claim: The Enid Blyton adaptation The Magic Faraway Tree was 2026's live-action exception, well received and highly profitable on its March UK release, with a US release following, and its distinguishing feature is a determined rejection of all things modern.
insights.speaker: Alexander Larman
insights.so_what: Anti-modern, anti-tech framing is a commercially validated positioning for family films — watch the US release as the test of whether it travels.
insights.quote: The exception this year in live-action cinema has been the Enid Blyton adaptation The Magic Faraway Tree, which was both well-received and, crucially, made a great deal of money when it was released in March in Britain.
insights.locator: The exception this year in live-action cinema

insights.claim: The Magic Faraway Tree's emotional climax about never being able to go home again moved the adults in the audience to tears while leaving children unaffected, because children have no experience of loss to project onto it.
insights.speaker: Alexander Larman
insights.so_what: The commercial payload of nostalgic family cinema targets the paying adult, not the child — a distinction that explains which films actually sell tickets.
insights.quote: Most of the adults in the cinema, myself included, were quietly sobbing, struck by the evocation of how painful it can be to grow up. But our children, for whom adulthood looms far and distant in the future, did not find it affecting
